---
framework: Behavioral Economics
---

# A trip-wire offer that pays for the funnel

The marketing team's lowest-priced item, a small accessory priced close to cost, is not expected to make money on its own, and everyone on the team already knows this going in. Its entire job is to get a new customer to complete a first purchase at all, crossing the psychological and logistical threshold of entering payment details and receiving a first delivery, since the data consistently shows that a customer who has bought once, at any price, is dramatically more likely to buy again than one who has never bought at all.

The item itself is chosen for being cheap, low-risk, and genuinely useful enough that the customer does not feel tricked, not for being profitable. The real return shows up two or three purchases later, once the customer has moved on to full-margin items, and the team tracks that later return carefully, because the trip-wire item's own margin, taken in isolation, would make it look like a bad product worth dropping rather than the deliberate draw it actually is.
